title: The independent-approval check

story: Monday afternoon. Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, has opened PR #2512 for RH-1234, the ticket you wrote and assigned to it. Byte, our review agent, reads the diff and approves. You look at the screenshots, like what you see, and approve too. GitHub now shows two approvals, the ruleset asks for one, the checks are green, and the merge button turns green.

Look at who approved. Byte is an agent, so its approval says nothing about whether a person checked the work. You are the person who asked for the change and who wants it merged most. GitHub has a rule that authors cannot approve their own pull requests, but the author here is the agents' bot account, not you, so that rule never applies. Two approvals, and no independent person has looked at the code.
hook.question: How do we make sure the one approval that counts comes from a person who did not ask for the work?

read.h: GitHub knows the author, not the asker
p: GitHub can only reason about what it sees: who opened the pull request, who pushed commits, who reviewed. On an agent's pull request the author is rhino-ai-agents[bot], so GitHub's own rule against self-approval protects nothing, and a ruleset cannot say "not this person" either. The fix is a required check of our own: a small program that runs in a GitHub Actions job on every pull request and every review, reads the facts through GitHub's API, and fails when the only approvals come from the wrong people. The ruleset then requires it by name, exactly like the unit tests.

The program still needs to know who asked. That information lives in Jira, not GitHub: the requester is the person who assigned the ticket to Nova, or the routine's owner when a routine opened the pull request (a routine is Nova started by an event, such as a red build). So the orchestrator, the service that runs every agent's work, writes it into the pull request body as one line at the end, Requested-by: @sean, and the check reads that line.

"The requester" is really a set of people, and each member is there because of a way to cheat. The pull request's author is in it. On an agent's pull request, so is the login on the Requested-by line. So is anyone who pushed a commit, because they wrote part of the change and cannot review their own part. And so is anyone who edited the pull request body, because otherwise the requester could change the line to Requested-by: @dana and then approve as if they were someone else.

One more rule makes the set safe: an agent's pull request without a Requested-by line fails. A check that cannot find the requester must not guess, and it must not quietly pass, because a missing line would then be the easiest way around the whole check. Engineers call this failing closed: when in doubt, the answer is no, and a person looks.

notes.text: The line must stand alone at the start of a line (the m flag), so a mention inside a sentence does not count.
Failing closed: no line, no pass. The job shows this message, so the reviewer knows what is missing.
Logins are compared in lower case, because GitHub treats Sean and sean as the same person.

p: Now the reviews. GitHub returns every review on the pull request, oldest first, and a reviewer can change their mind, so the check keeps only each reviewer's latest decisive review: approved, changes requested or dismissed. A plain comment afterwards does not cancel an approval. Then an approval counts only if three things are true. It is on the head commit, the newest commit of the pull request, so nobody can approve version two and have version three merged. It comes from a user, not a bot or an app, so Byte's approval never counts. And the reviewer is not in the requester set.

If at least one approval passes all of that, the check passes. The lab runs the check on three snapshots of PR #2512: Monday's, with only Byte and you (login sean); Tuesday's, after Dana, a teammate, approved; and one where Dana approved the commit before the last push.

notes.text: COMMENTED is missing on purpose: a comment after an approval leaves the approval standing.
A later decisive review from the same person replaces the earlier one.
Approvals on older commits do not count.
GitHub marks apps and bots with a different type, so agents can never be the one approval.

read.see:
prs/2512-monday.json: requesters rhino-ai-agents[bot], sean
FAIL  no approval from someone outside the requesters on the latest commit
prs/2512-tuesday.json: requesters rhino-ai-agents[bot], sean
PASS  independent approval from dana
prs/2512-late.json: requesters rhino-ai-agents[bot], sean
FAIL  no approval from someone outside the requesters on the latest commit

deeper.h: Go deeper: where the check runs, and why not in fcp
p: The logic lives in the platform repo, ai-agents, and runs from a container image pinned by its digest, the image's content hash. fcp only has a thin caller workflow, pinned to one commit, that starts it on pull_request events (opened, edited, synchronize, reopened, ready for review) and on pull_request_review events (submitted, edited, dismissed), with read-only permissions. The edited event matters: changing the body re-runs the check. The split matters even more. If the check's code lived in fcp, an agent's pull request could change the program that judges it. In ai-agents, a pull request on fcp cannot touch it.

The ruleset already has a setting that sounds similar, require_last_push_approval, which stops the person who pushed last from approving. The check is wider: it covers every person who pushed, not only the last one, plus the requester and the body editors. Once the check exists, DevOps adds its exact name, as GitHub shows it on a pull request, to the ruleset's required checks.

lab.title: Prove whose approval counts
lab.goal: Run the independent-approval check on three snapshots of one pull request, then write the tests that catch the two ways people really try to get around it.

guess.q: On PR #2512, Requested-by is @sean, which is you. You open the description, change the line to Requested-by: @dana (a teammate), and then approve. The check reads only the author and the Requested-by line. Does it pass?

options.text: No, because you are the requester.
options.why: The check no longer sees that: the line now says dana, and you are not the author. Unless body editors are in the requester set, it cannot tell.

options.text: Yes: the line says dana, and you look like an independent reviewer.
options.why: That is why anyone who edited the body joins the requester set. Without it, one edit turns the requester into a reviewer.

options.text: No, GitHub refuses edits to the body of a bot's pull request.
options.why: People with write access can edit any pull request's description. The check has to handle it.

follow.say: Make a scratch folder. type: module lets the tests use top-level await later.
follow.do: mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/scratch/g0-3 && cd ~/academy-labs/scratch/g0-3 && npm init -y > /dev/null && npm pkg set type=module

follow.say: Save the check, the two functions from the lesson in one file.
Save a small runner that does what the GitHub job does after it has read the API: build the requester set and look for one independent approval.
Save three snapshots of PR #2512, as the API would describe them.
follow.do:
mkdir -p prs
B='"pr": { "user": { "login": "rhino-ai-agents[bot]" }, "body": "Adds the No projects yet card.\n\nRequested-by: @sean" }, "headSha": "c3", "commitAuthors": ["rhino-ai-agents[bot]"], "bodyEditors": []'
cat > prs/2512-monday.json <<EOF
{ $B, "reviews": [
  { "state": "APPROVED", "commit_id": "c3", "user": { "login": "byte-review[bot]", "type": "Bot" } },
  { "state": "APPROVED", "commit_id": "c3", "user": { "login": "sean", "type": "User" } } ] }
EOF
cat > prs/2512-tuesday.json <<EOF
{ $B, "reviews": [
  { "state": "APPROVED", "commit_id": "c3", "user": { "login": "byte-review[bot]", "type": "Bot" } },

lab.build: Write independent-approval.test.ts with node:test. Load the code under test with const impl = await import(process.env.IMPL ?? "./independent-approval.ts") so the same tests can judge another version later. Write one test for each case: a human PR approved by a teammate passes; an agent PR approved only by its requester fails; the requester edits the body to name someone else, then approves, and it fails; an approval on an older commit fails; a bot approval is ignored; a reviewer who pushed a fix is not independent; an agent PR without a Requested-by line throws MissingRequester. Run node --test --test-reporter=spec independent-approval.test.ts.
checks: node --test --test-reporter=spec independent-approval.test.ts shows 7 tests and 7 passing.
The body-edit test passes the editor's login in bodyEditors and expects no independent approver.
The bot test uses a review whose user.type is Bot.
The missing-line test uses assert.throws with impl.MissingRequester.
lab.fix: A teammate finds the requester set "too clever" and keeps only the author and the Requested-by person. Make their version with mkdir -p fix && sed 's/\[...people, ...commitAuthors, ...bodyEditors\]/[...people]/' independent-approval.ts > fix/independent-approval.ts, then run your tests against it with IMPL=./fix/independent-approval.ts node --test --test-reporter=spec independent-approval.test.ts. Two tests should fail. For each, describe the real trick it would let through, step by step, on PR #2512.
explain: Why can't GitHub's own rule against self-approval protect an agent's pull request?
Why are people who pushed a commit and people who edited the body part of the requester set?
Why does the check fail when an agent's pull request has no Requested-by line, instead of passing or guessing?
lab.done: Your seven tests pass against the real check and two of them fail against the teammate's version.

check.q: You requested Nova's pull request. Byte approved it and you approved it. Why does the independent-approval check fail?

options.text: Because there are two approvals and exactly one is required.
options.why: More approvals never fail the check. What matters is whether one of them is independent.

options.text: Because Byte is a bot and you are the requester, so neither approval is independent.
options.why: Bot approvals never count, and the requester's never does. One approval from someone else, such as Dana, a teammate, would pass.

options.text: Because Byte must approve after you, not before.
options.why: Order does not matter here. Each approval is judged on who gave it and on which commit.

check.q: Dana, a teammate, approved PR #2512. Then Nova pushed one more commit to fix a lint warning. What does the check say now, and why?

options.why: Dana approved an older commit. Approvals count only on the head commit.

options.text: It fails until Dana, or someone else outside the requesters, approves the new head commit.
options.why: Otherwise version two could be approved and version three merged.

options.text: It fails for good, because Nova pushed after the approval.
options.why: Nothing is permanent: a new approval on the new head commit passes it.

check.q: Why does the orchestrator, the service that runs every agent's work, write a Requested-by line into the pull request body?

options.text: Because who asked for the work is known in Jira, not in GitHub, and the check needs it.
options.why: GitHub sees the bot as the author. The line carries the requester from the hand-off into the place the check can read.

options.text: So GitHub assigns the requester as a reviewer automatically.
options.why: The line is plain text. GitHub does nothing with it; our check reads it.

options.text: So the requester gets credit for the commit.
options.why: The line exists to exclude the requester from approving, not to give credit.

p: The check is ai-agents/checks/src/independent-approval.ts with node:test cases in ai-agents/checks/test/independent-approval.test.ts. A reusable workflow, ai-agents/.github/workflows/independent-approval.yml, runs it on fcp-runner-set from the ai-agents-checks image pinned by digest (node /app/dist/independent-approval.js). fcp gets a thin caller, .github/workflows/independent-approval.yml, pinned by SHA, with contents: read and pull-requests: read. DevOps adds the check's exact name (for example independent-approval / check) to the main ruleset. Nova's hand-off writes the Requested-by line; routines write their owner.

The ready gate in G4-27 waits for the required checks before it marks a draft ready. This check can only pass after a person approves, and nobody approves a draft, so the gate leaves this one check out by name; otherwise the PR would stay a draft forever.

tickets.why: This lesson: the requester set, the approval rules, the reusable workflow, the fcp caller and the tests.
Where the rule 'the requester never approves' and the definition of the requester were agreed.
The ready gate, which must not wait for this check on a draft.

words.plain: The person who asked for the work: whoever assigned the ticket to Nova, or a routine's owner.
Everyone who cannot give the one approval: author, Requested-by person, every pusher, every body editor.
The last line the orchestrator writes in an agent's pull request body, naming the requester.
The newest commit on the pull request; only approvals of it count.
When the check cannot be sure, it fails and a person looks, instead of passing.

review.q: List the four kinds of people in the requester set, and the trick each one blocks.
review.a: Author (self-approval), the Requested-by person (the asker approving their own agent's work), anyone who pushed (reviewing your own code), anyone who edited the body (rewriting Requested-by to someone else).

review.q: What three conditions must an approval meet to count, apart from the reviewer not being a requester?
review.a: It is the reviewer's latest decisive review and it is APPROVED, it is on the head commit, and the reviewer is a User, not a bot or app.

review.q: Why does the check's code live in ai-agents and not in fcp?
review.a: Code in fcp could be changed by the pull request it judges, including an agent's. In ai-agents, running from a pinned image, an fcp pull request cannot touch it.

remember: GitHub knows the author, not the asker: our check reads the requester from the pull request and counts only a person's approval of the latest commit from outside the requester set.
